item.description:

item.title: 🔵 Building the agent and securing it
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Earlier this year, I wrote about how vibe coding an AI governance platform forced me to rethink governance itself. Building agents took the problem much further.

When I built the platform, I was the operator. I described what I wanted. The model generated code. I tested it. That loop was fast, sometimes uncomfortably fast, but the accountability was always clear. I was making the decisions. The model was executing them.

Agents changed that relationship fundamentally.

An agent does not wait for instructions. It receives an objective, decides how to pursue it, selects tools, accesses data, takes actions and reports back when it is finished. Sometimes it finishes correctly. Sometimes it does not. And sometimes it does something you never asked it to do at all.

item.title: 🟠 OpenAI’s models are deliberately breaking their misalignment monitoring systems
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

AI agents are getting more inventive in finding ways to circumvent safeguards to prevent bad behavior, OpenAI has revealed.

On Tuesday, it reported two incidents, both involving the agent disabling or interfering with its alignment monitoring, and in one case directly lying about having done so. 

“In two internal coding tasks, agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes,” the OpenAI blog post said. “A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that it had not removed the monitor.”

item.description:

Organizations are scrambling to protect themselves following the disclosure of two critical vulnerabilities in commonly used code that powers much of the internet. The flaws discovered in the PHP scripting language could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

On Wednesday morning, the PHP Foundation released patches for affected versions, and said it is “imperative” that organizations running PHP patch immediately. It said that all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It considers the risk highest for mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs.

In response to the disclosures, some government websites in Europe, including those in the Netherlands and Finland, as well as those of other organizations worldwide, went offline as a precautionary measure.

item.title: 🔵 Autonomy creep: how AI quietly gains more authority than CIOs intend
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Few CIOs are likely to suddenly decide to give an AI agent broad authority over corporate systems. The more likely path to autonomy is far less dramatic. An agent starts with a narrow task. It proves useful, so another system is connected. It then needs more data, so another permission is added. Then human approval becomes a bottleneck, so the organization removes it, and exceptions that once went to people start being handled automatically.

Each decision may be sensible in isolation. Taken together, however, they can leave an agent with considerably more authority than anyone originally envisioned.

That’s the danger of autonomy creep. And as enterprises move from AI systems that recommend actions to agents that execute them, CIOs need to govern not only what those agents were originally designed to do, but what they have gradually become capable of doing.

CIOs bring a lot to their new jobs: decades of leadership, transformation, pattern-recognition, and outcomes. But none of that matters in your new job. During a time of generalized uncertainty, your team — and every stakeholder — needs to trust you more than anything. But how do you build that trust in a new environment, and as quickly as possible? For Cengage CIO Ken Grady, the best approach is an architectural one.

item.description:

For years, disaster recovery was built around a relatively simple question: How quickly can we get the business back online?

That question still matters. But for today’s CIO, it is no longer enough.

Enterprise technology environments have become too dynamic to define recovery simply as restoring applications, reconnecting infrastructure and resuming operations. Applications span on-premises infrastructure, cloud environments and SaaS platforms. Identities and permissions are constantly changing. Employees introduce new tools and automation into workflows, sometimes without IT knowing about them. AI is accelerating that pace of change even further.

As a CIO, I see this complexity firsthand. My organization is navigating its own transformation while modernizing the technology that supports the business. item.title: 🔵 The inference path is where AI value is won or lost
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

As organizations incorporate AI into their environments, they’re hyper-focused on the AI model. Many executives I talk to spend a lot of time considering what model they should purchase from which vendor. They’re also concerned about which use case they should implement first.

Yet the reality is that AI models are swappable components. The vast majority of organizations are using multiple AI models, switching them out for their specific needs based on cost, accuracy, and security. It’s the right thing to do; organizations with architectures that make it difficult to swap out AI models are making the wrong bet.

What can’t be swapped out is your inference path—or everything that happens between a user’s intent and the model’s output. This includes the retrieval layer that decides what context the model sees. It includes the routing logic that chooses what model handles which request. It includes the identity that travels with the call. On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables.

Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000. Its chief executive, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that the cold chain held in most of them. Only a minority reacted too slowly and lost stock, and he credited store staff and refrigeration contractors for the difference. Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw away everything. item.title: 🔵 OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices.

A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems.

Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL).

item.description:

Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands.
